text: Your heart beats about one hundred thousand times a day, and every single beat starts with a tiny electrical spark. So where does that spark come from, and how does it spread so perfectly? Let's unfold the heart's electrical system.

Unlike the muscles in your arm, your heart doesn't wait for a signal from your brain. It makes its own electrical signals, and sends them through a built in wiring system, called the conduction system. This wiring makes sure the upper chambers, the atria, squeeze first, and the lower chambers, the ventricles, squeeze right after.

Every beat starts here, in the sinoatrial node, or S A node. It's a small cluster of special cells in the wall of the right atrium, near where the superior vena cava enters. The S A node is the heart's natural pacemaker. At rest, it fires about sixty to one hundred times a minute.
The signal spreads across both atria like a wave. The atria contract, and top up the ventricles with blood.

Next, the signal reaches the atrioventricular node, or A V node, which sits between the atria and the ventricles. Here, the signal is briefly delayed. This short pause gives the atria time to finish emptying, so the ventricles are full before they squeeze.

From the A V node, the signal rushes down the bundle of His, which splits into the right and left bundle branches, running along the septum. Finally, it spreads through the Purkinje fibers, into the walls of the ventricles. Both ventricles contract together, starting near the bottom of the heart, and squeeze blood out to the lungs and to the body.

And if the S A node fails, the heart has backups. The A V node can take over, at about forty to sixty beats a minute. And the ventricles can make their own rhythm, at about twenty to forty beats a minute. That's slower, but it can still keep blood moving.

We can actually see this electrical activity with an electrocardiogram, or E C G. The P wave shows the atria being activated. The Q R S complex shows the ventricles being activated, just before they contract. And the T wave shows the ventricles recovering, getting ready for the next beat.
Your nervous system can change the pace. During exercise or stress, sympathetic nerves speed up the S A node. When you rest, the vagus nerve slows it down.

So, to sum up. S A node, atria, A V node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers, and ventricles. One spark, perfectly timed, about a hundred thousand times a day. In the next video, we'll see what happens during a heart attack.
